title: LawTech Talks: How AI is reshaping collaboration across the legal ecosystem — CJ Saretto (Axiom) & Ashleigh Whittaker (Harvey Australia) with Jerome Doraisamy (Lawyers Weekly)

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

kp.k: AI shifts attention from individual tasks to service delivery
kp.d: Whittaker characterises 2026 as a shift from the task-specific AI conversations of 12 or 24 months earlier toward how law firms deliver value to in-house teams. Saretto says in-house teams see AI as enabling more work internally and changing expectations of law firms, alternative legal service providers and e-discovery firms. These are speakers’ market observations, not quantified findings.
qs: A lot of in-house teams see AI as a big superpower.
They see it as a way to do more in-house  that they always would have liked to do in-house before.
So I think we were looking back 12 or 24 months ago  and the conversation was more around  what is AI bringing to the work we do individually day-to-day?
what is the value that you're delivering  as a law firm to the in-house team?

kp.k: Shared workspaces replace fragmented collaboration with contextual legal work
kp.d: Whittaker contrasts email, Teams, calls and separately produced work with Harvey shared spaces, which she describes as matter-specific environments combining data, precedents, legislation, workflows, playbooks, review tables and co-editable outputs. She says outside counsel and in-house lawyers can engage with work in real time. She does not claim traditional collaboration necessarily creates AI-specific difficulties, instead presenting shared spaces as an improvement.
qs: really, we're talking about a combination  of fragmented tools.
I don't know that it necessarily creates difficulties,  but I do think that AI opens up a new way to do this better.
really a context aware system for a matter.
I also have the ability to run workflows, playbooks,  and potentially within Harvey, we call them review tables,  the ability to extract insights at scale.

kp.k: Permissions and auditability underpin cross-organisational collaboration
kp.d: Whittaker describes governance, auditability and access controls as foundational to shared spaces. Matter owners can give clients, barristers, experts and working lawyers different rights, including viewing, editing or running workflows without seeing their underlying configuration. These are vendor descriptions of functionality, not independent evidence of confidentiality or security outcomes.
qs: at the foundation is governance,  auditability, permissions and access controls.
I might be able to run a particular AI workflow  but not actually see what sits behind the hood.
every individual that enters that space  might have different levels of access.

kp.k: Persistent matter knowledge supports reuse and acquisition integration
kp.d: Saretto contrasts client access through firms’ document portals with shared storage, generated artifacts and reusable workflows. He argues these could support comparison across transactions, reuse of diligence frameworks and less repeated work across providers. He identifies acquisition integration as a particularly promising use case because teams need prior analysis, decision context and workflows they can rerun or modify; he presents this chiefly as an opportunity rather than a measured result.
qs: now you can start to leverage knowledge  across matters in a really different way.
Could we just apply that analysis framework  to this new transaction?
it's even better if you actually have access  to the workflow so that you can rerun them  or modify pieces of the analysis

kp.k: Unbundling reallocates work among firms, in-house teams and ALSPs
kp.d: Saretto argues that sending an entire matter to one firm has often reflected workflow convenience rather than cost effectiveness. Shared assets could let lower-cost providers handle document review and analysis while expensive partners advise on consequential results. He illustrates the proposed arbitrage with potentially $1,500-an-hour associates versus $300–$400-an-hour senior attorneys through an alternative method; these are illustrative rates, not demonstrated savings. He asserts that most outsourced work is non-extraordinary work that in-house departments lack capacity or expertise to perform.
qs: am I just sending a matter to one shop for convenience?
That's not the most cost effective way  to handle all the different aspects,  but it was the most efficient way  to handle the workflow before.
maybe $1,500 an hour associates to do that analysis  when you could be using 300, $400 an hour,  very senior attorneys to do that analysis  through an alternative method.
It's work that the in-house team would do if it could,  but it doesn't have the capacity or the expertise to do it.

kp.k: Business users can self-serve within approved legal playbooks
kp.d: Whittaker reports emerging uses of shared spaces as internal legal help desks, including policy templates for HR and NDA playbooks for sales, business development and procurement. Her proposed mechanism is context-aware self-service under in-house-approved standards, potentially developed with external counsel, with escalation to legal or finance when flagged rather than routing every request through those teams.
qs: can shared spaces be that legal help desk for my team?
And now HR or employment can self-serve  to identify how to answer certain questions.
So they're flagged when you need to send things  to legal or finance,  but it's not going every single time through that team.

kp.d: Whittaker reports a global law firm building approximately 25 custom diligence workflows for a private equity client, eventually spanning the full deal cycle. These vendor-reported examples describe self-service deployment but provide no named customers, evaluation design or quantified outcome measures.

those workflows eventually covered their full deal cycle  from start to finish.

kp.d: Saretto reports that Axiom’s client engagements involve configuring AI around distinct departmental standards, processes and workflows, with clients requesting that configurations remain after engagements end. He distinguishes technical configuration from changing working habits and recommends pairing an AI-experienced attorney with an in-house attorney on real work. He describes this one-to-one transfer as protecting privilege and confidentiality, without providing comparative adoption results.

kp.k: Future operating models require joint design amid uncertainty
kp.d: Whittaker recommends that in-house teams and law firms jointly discuss service delivery, embedded expertise and appropriate revenue models rather than redesigning them separately. Saretto endorses moving at a mutually comfortable pace and acknowledges that he cannot specify the right future combination of AI and human roles. His expectation of dramatic change over the next two years is explicitly a prediction, not a finding.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: CJ Saretto claims AI-enabled collaboration can unbundle matters, move more work in-house or to ALSPs, and reserve law firms for work requiring their expertise.
pts.d: Saretto describes in-house teams viewing AI as a way to undertake work they previously outsourced. Shared control of matter assets would let clients divide assignments among their own lawyers, lower-cost providers such as Axiom, and premium law-firm advisers rather than instructing one firm for convenience. He identifies document review, acquisition diligence and integration as leading opportunities, and says sharing across providers can avoid repeated work. These are proposed operating-model and cost benefits, not quantified savings demonstrated in the episode.

pts.k: Ashleigh Whittaker claims shared AI workspaces change legal collaboration from fragmented exchanges to a common environment for doing the work; Saretto adds that they enable reuse of knowledge across matters.
pts.d: Whittaker contrasts email, Teams, calls and work on separate computers with a matter-specific environment containing source material, workflows, playbooks and co-editable outputs. She says outside counsel and clients can engage with work in real time and clients can use the firm's AI tools. Saretto extends this to retaining transaction knowledge, reusing diligence frameworks and carrying analysis into integration. Whittaker does not claim traditional methods necessarily become dysfunctional under AI; she argues AI offers a better alternative.

pts.k: Whittaker claims shared spaces enable business-user self-service; Saretto predicts this will spread from NDAs to broader commercial contracting.
pts.d: Whittaker describes legal help desks, policy templates and approved NDA playbooks through which HR, sales, business development and procurement can obtain answers or progress work without routing every request through legal. Exceptions would be flagged for legal or finance. Saretto predicts MSAs, statements of work and sales order forms will follow. This is a move beyond lawyer augmentation toward direct business reliance on configured AI for routine work, with human escalation rather than universal lawyer review. Saretto conditions it on client-specific standards and confidence in the system's reasoning and escalation decisions.

pts.k: Whittaker claims self-service legal workflows are prompting early exploration of subscriptions, fixed fees and usage-based licensing.
pts.d: Whittaker says firms are beginning to discuss how to monetise expertise embedded in client-run workflows, rather than simply giving away work. She offers fund-formation subscriptions and licensing a deals-benchmark workflow each time it is run as possible models. Auditability would allow firms to track usage. Saretto separately says AI is beginning to influence Axiom's service charges. Neither speaker claims a profession-wide replacement of hourly billing or provides revenue results.

pts.k: Saretto claims bespoke configuration and lawyer-to-lawyer skills transfer support workflow adoption; Whittaker reports emerging legal-engineer and champion roles.
pts.d: Saretto distinguishes configuring AI around each client's standards from getting lawyers to change their practices. He says Axiom's repeated engagements make subsequent implementations faster and that side-by-side work on real matters transfers skills effectively. Whittaker agrees that habit change and social proof matter, and reports customers creating roles combining legal subject-matter knowledge with AI-system expertise. These claims concern implementation services and changing roles, not measured employment displacement.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Whittaker supports the workflow claims with two unnamed client examples and the adoption claim with a bank-lawyer anecdote.
pts.d: Whittaker reports a global law firm building approximately 25 diligence workflows for a private equity client, ultimately covering the deal cycle, and a law-firm employment team building more than a dozen HR workflows for a global retailer, including offer letters, performance plans and termination checklists. These illustrate reported implementations, without named clients, outcome measurements or independent validation. Her account of a bank lawyer becoming a power user after sustained experimentation is an adoption anecdote relayed by Whittaker, not a separately interviewed source or controlled finding. No model benchmarks, error rates or verification results are supplied.

pts.k: Saretto grounds his claims in Axiom's engagement experience and illustrative pricing; the broader transformation predictions are explicitly expectations.
pts.d: Saretto says Axiom has experimented with deploying AI in client engagements and measuring returns, but discloses no measurements, methods or sample sizes. He cites client requests to retain configurations and describes recurring implementation lessons. His claim that most outsourced work is non-extraordinary is attributed to Axiom's categorisation without supporting distribution data. The comparison between $1,500-an-hour associates and $300–$400-an-hour senior attorneys is illustrative, not a reported comparative study; the currency is not specified. The episode is produced in partnership with Axiom, and both substantive speakers represent businesses involved in the offerings discussed: Axiom is an ALSP and Harvey a legal-AI vendor.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The speakers frame 2026 as a shift from individual AI tasks toward service-delivery transformation, with commercial models still emerging and substantial further change anticipated within two years.
pts.d: Whittaker contrasts the conversation in 2026 with the preceding 12–24 months, when attention centred on individual tasks. She presents shared-space implementations and emerging roles as current observations, while describing pricing changes as early-stage exploration. Saretto predicts a markedly different landscape two years after the episode, approximately 2028, but explicitly acknowledges uncertainty about the right operating model. His prediction of wider self-service contracting has no specific deadline.

pts.k: The proposed benefits depend on controlled access, matter context, customised standards, user adoption and agreement between clients and providers.
pts.d: Whittaker identifies governance, auditability and differentiated permissions as foundations for sharing work with clients, advisers, barristers and experts. Saretto links unbundling to control of matter assets and links business-user automation to making AI reflect the department's own standards. Both describe adoption as requiring behavioural change and joint discussion of delivery and revenue models. They do not supply an accuracy threshold or a specified human-verification procedure for outputs; the express safeguard for self-service examples is escalation when needed.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claims primarily concern corporate legal departments, their business stakeholders and the provider ecosystem serving them.
pts.d: In-house legal departments are presented as gaining capacity, control of matter knowledge and sourcing options. Corporate HR, sales, business development and procurement teams gain potential self-service access. Law firms may retain high-stakes advisory work while supplying embedded expertise through workflows and reconsidering pricing. ALSPs such as Axiom may receive unbundled work and provide configuration and adoption support; Harvey supplies the software environment rather than acting as an ALSP. Barristers and experts may participate through controlled access. Lawyers' workflows and legal-engineering roles change, but the source makes no quantified staffing forecast. The concrete examples concern private equity, acquisitions, a global retailer and banking, not unmet civil legal need or access to justice.
